claims.statement: dcode installs through the bundled curl installer and normally launches an interactive Textual TUI; it can instead run one headless task with `-n` or serve ACP over stdio with `--acp`.
Project artifacts are read before tool approval UI, so approvals do not make an untrusted checkout safe; use a remote sandbox to isolate execution from the host.

Normal operations fail closed with exit 78 when managed configuration cannot be enforced, except diagnostic `config`, `doctor`, `auth path`, and help paths; thread listing and deletion dispatch without launching an agent.
Headless-only output, turn, timeout, and rubric controls require a headless task; shell is disabled without a shell allow-list, and turn or timeout budget expiry uses exit 124.
Interactive approval has Manual, Auto, and YOLO modes; invalid persisted values fall back to Manual, Shift+Tab omits unavailable modes, and YOLO requires a versioned acknowledgement.

Interactive and headless clients start a temporary local LangGraph runtime via `server_session`, serialize resolved server configuration, preflight an explicit MCP configuration, wait for the graph, bind the RemoteAgent to the project workspace, and clean up failed startup or normal teardown.

Session checkpoints reside in cached global SQLite state; UUID7 thread IDs are naturally time-sortable, and thread listing uses a covering index to avoid reading checkpoint blobs while retaining a slower correct fallback if index creation fails.

TUI resume resolves bare `-r` as the recent thread and explicit IDs as named threads, offers a stored-cwd switch, suggests similar missing IDs, and falls back to a fresh thread on a miss or database error; headless always creates a new thread.

Hook handlers run trusted user-privilege commands with JSON lifecycle payloads; project hooks require workspace trust, matching handlers execute concurrently but reduce project-user-plugin, and exit code 2 is event-specific blocking.

Explicit MCP configuration has highest precedence, `--no-mcp` disables MCP loading, and project MCP servers require trust; experimental project Python extensions also require trust and extension tools are not automatically in dcode's human-approval map.
A bare `--sandbox` resolves the configured default while an omitted sandbox remains local; sandbox ID, snapshot, and setup options select or provision the remote environment.
Focused unit tests exercise thread-list cwd handling, persisted cwd behavior, and thread deletion cleanup of offloaded history.

The temporary LangGraph runtime used by TUI and headless clients listens on loopback `127.0.0.1` with an ephemeral port by default; after the `agent` graph is ready, the client creates and workspace-binds a `RemoteAgent` with a configuration fingerprint.

ACP mode does not use the temporary loopback `server_session`: it constructs a model, loads MCP tools, opens the SQLite checkpointer, builds agents for ACP session contexts, and serves the supplied ACP server through `run_acp_agent`, with MCP cleanup in `finally`.

The server graph factory reads serialized `ServerConfig` from environment, but execution with runtime context requires a thread ID and workspace context, resolves that thread's persisted workspace binding, verifies its configuration fingerprint and payload, and selects a cached or newly built workspace runtime.

Piped stdin is capped at 10 MiB and is routed by precedence to an existing headless task, an interactive initial prompt, an auto-detected startup skill prompt, or a new headless task; explicit `--stdin` requires non-terminal stdin.

ACP dependency import failures and MCP configuration loading failures report exit code 1 before serving, while an exception during ACP serving is reported as an ACP server failure and also yields exit code 1.
Workspace runtimes are cached with an LRU limit of 32; a sandbox backend is process-wide, so a binding for another workspace is rejected after the sandbox is claimed.

The normal remote client forwards workspace context on every stream, converts server messages and HITL interrupts into client values, and requires a thread ID; the TUI requests message, update, and custom streams and resumes after user interaction.

The server builds a workspace runtime from a frozen workspace environment and credentials, creates built-in and MCP tools and an optional sandbox, then gives `create_cli_agent` the resulting resources; its cached runtime shares the graph backend and offload operation.

The compaction-resume integration test persists a thread through one temporary server, runs `/offload` in a fresh production-style app with no client-owned backend, and verifies the offloaded archive remains readable through later server agents.

The end-to-end agent tests deliberately use asynchronous graph invocation because production entrypoints stream, and verify both tool traversal and summarization that offloads conversation history through the backend.
